stem: A code first reverses a four-letter word, then shifts the first and third letters forward one place and the second and fourth letters backward one place, wrapping between A and Z. What is the code for ZONE?
explanation: Reverse ZONE to ENOZ, then apply +1, −1, +1, −1: E→F, N→M, O→P, Z→Y. FMPY requires applying both operations in order; shifting first would produce a different result.

stem: Six files A, B, C, D, E, F are processed once each. A is before C; C is immediately before E; B is before D; F is immediately after B. If E is fifth, which file must be sixth?
explanation: E fifth forces C fourth. The B–F block must occupy positions 1–2 or 2–3: positions 3–4 are blocked by C and 5–6 by E. A must fill the other position before C, so D occupies sixth. Both B,F,A,C,E,D and A,B,F,C,E,D satisfy the constraints.

stem: A parcel is released if and only if its form is signed and either it passes testing or it has an exemption. A suspended parcel is never released. Parcel K was released without passing testing. Which set of conclusions must hold?

choices.text: K has an exemption and is not suspended, but its form may be unsigned.
K has a signed form, has an exemption, and is not suspended.
K has a signed form and is not suspended, but it may lack an exemption.
K has a signed form and an exemption, but it may be suspended.

explanation: Release implies a signed form and at least one of testing or exemption. Since testing did not occur successfully, the exemption is necessary. Suspension would rule out the observed release, so K is not suspended. Each distractor drops one necessary conclusion.

stem: Five people A, B, C, D, E sit left to right in five seats. B sits immediately to the right of A. C is not in the first seat. D sits to the left of C. E sits to the right of B, and D sits next to E. Which list contains all and only the people who could sit in the middle seat?
explanation: If the A–B block starts in seat 2, E must be in seat 4 or 5; D must then be in seat 1 to precede C, so D cannot be next to E. If the block starts in seat 3, E is fifth and D cannot be next to E because B is fourth. Starting in seat 4 leaves no place for E after B. Thus A,B occupy 1,2. The remaining conditions allow exactly A,B,D,E,C and A,B,E,D,C. Their middle occupants are D and E.

stem: Every logged record is encrypted. No encrypted record is public. Some remote records are public, and every remote record is signed. Which conclusion must follow?

Every record that is not logged is public.

explanation: Take a remote public record whose existence is guaranteed. It is signed because it is remote, and it cannot be encrypted because it is public. It therefore cannot be logged, since all logged records are encrypted. This proves some signed records are not logged, without excluding other signed records from encryption or asserting that any logged record exists.

stem: Exactly one of P and Q is selected. Selecting P requires R; selecting R requires S. S is selected if and only if T is selected. T is not selected. Which pair of conclusions must follow?

choices.text: P is selected; R is not selected.
Q is selected; R is selected.
Q is selected; R is not selected.
Neither P nor Q is selected.

explanation: From not T and S iff T, S is not selected. R would require S, so R is not selected. P would require R, so P is not selected. Exactly one of P and Q then forces Q. This uses the requirements backwards by contraposition, not the invalid reversal of an implication.

stem: An editor proofreads a report for typing errors without checking its claims. A second editor fact-checks claims without changing the prose. Which pair of findings maps to the two processes in that order?

choices.text: An incorrect date in the source record; an omitted letter in a word
An omitted letter in a word; a claim contradicted by the cited record
A claim contradicted by the cited record; a disputed interpretation of policy
An omitted letter in a word; a smoother rephrasing of the same claim

explanation: The first editor's target is the text as typed, so an omitted letter fits proofreading. The second checks claims against evidence, so contradiction by a cited record fits fact-checking. Reversing those targets fails their stated order; changing wording for smoothness does not check truth. The correct first target also appears with an incorrect second target, and the correct second target with an incorrect first, so both mappings must be checked.

stem: Six runners A, B, C, D, E, and F stand in an unknown front-to-rear order. C is immediately ahead of D; A is ahead of E; E is ahead of C; B is last; F is neither first nor last. B then moves to the front, and C leaves. Everyone else retains relative order. Which runners could now occupy third place?
explanation: Before the moves, the chain A before E before C immediately before D and B last allows only A-E-C-D-F-B, A-E-F-C-D-B, and A-F-E-C-D-B: F can be inserted in the three permitted non-end gaps without splitting C-D. Moving B first and removing C yields B-A-E-D-F, B-A-E-F-D, and B-A-F-E-D. The third runner can therefore be E or F, but not A or D. The initial order is not unique, so tracking one example would be insufficient.

stem: A lock code uses each of the digits 2, 4, and 7 exactly once. Exactly one of these three reports is false: (I) the first digit is 2; (II) 4 occurs before 7; (III) the last digit is not 2. A separate verified fact says that 7 is not first. Which digits could be in the middle?
explanation: Testing all six permutations against the verified fact and the count of false reports leaves 274 (I true, II false, III true) and 427 (I false, II true, III true). Code 247 makes all reports true; 472 makes I and III false; 724 and 742 violate the verified first-digit fact. The middle is therefore either 7 or 2. Treating a report as a verified fact, or accepting just one matching code, misses a permitted case.

stem: Four trains L, M, N, and P have distinct departure times. L departs before M; N departs before L; P departs before M. No other order is specified. Which trains could be the first to depart?
explanation: N must precede L, so L cannot be first; both L and P precede M, so M cannot be first. N,P,L,M is a valid order beginning with N, and P,N,L,M is a valid order beginning with P. Thus exactly N or P can be first; proving possibility requires a valid order, not assuming unspecified trains have a fixed position.

stem: A draft procedure says a desk must have a lamp or receive daylight; it does not require both. A supervisor adds that the lamp must be inspected whenever one is used. Desk R receives daylight and has no lamp. Desk S has an inspected lamp but no daylight. Which assessment follows from the combined rules?

Only S meets the rules, because adding an inspection rule makes a lamp compulsory.
Neither meets the rules, because each desk must have both lighting sources.
Both meet the rules; inspection is triggered by lamp use, not by the absence of daylight.

explanation: The lighting condition is inclusive or: either source suffices. R satisfies it with daylight and triggers no lamp inspection; S satisfies it with its inspected lamp. stem: All unit prices are positive. Three notebooks cost the same as two pens, and five pens cost the same as two folders. A kit contains exactly eight items, including at least one notebook, one pen, and one folder. Its total price equals the price of four folders. Which composition is possible?
explanation: Use a price unit of one-sixth of a pen: notebook, pen, and folder prices are 4, 6, and 15 units, so the kit costs 60 units. With counts n,p,f, n+p+f=8 and 4n+6p+15f=60. Subtracting four times the count equation gives 2p+11f=28. Thus f must be even; f=2 gives p=3 and n=3, while f≥4 forces p<0. The unique positive whole-number composition is 3,3,2. The alternatives all have eight items but cost 62, 58, and 78 units respectively.
